title: The First Stars and Galaxies
objective: After this level you can describe how the first stars and galaxies lit up the early universe.
summary: After the dark ages, massive stars of pure hydrogen and helium lit up and seeded space with heavier elements. Webb hunts their galaxies.

cards.headline: After its first light, the universe went dark for a long time.
cards.body: When the CMB broke free, there were no stars yet to shine. So who turned the lights on?

cards.headline: The cosmic dark ages
cards.body: Picture a universe with no stars at all: just cooling gas, mostly hydrogen and helium, drifting in the dark. Astronomers call this long stretch the cosmic dark ages. Gravity was busy, though, pulling the gas into collapsing clumps. Within a few hundred million years after the Big Bang, the first stars lit up. The longest blackout in history, ended by gravity.

cards.headline: Giants of two elements
cards.body: The first stars had a short ingredient list: only hydrogen and helium, since that’s nearly all the Big Bang had made. They’re thought to have been very massive and short-lived, the rock stars of the early universe. When they died, they made the first heavier elements and scattered them into space, seeding the gas that later stars and planets formed from. Live fast, die young, leave behind the makings of planets.

cards.headline: Finding the first galaxies
cards.body: How do you photograph the dawn? Light from these early galaxies has crossed so much expanding space that it has been stretched into infrared. So to find them, you hunt in infrared. Webb has already seen galaxies as they were only a few hundred million years after the Big Bang. Those are baby pictures of the universe, taken in a color your eyes can’t see.

cards.headline: First light: found
learned: The cosmic dark ages came before the first stars
The first stars were only hydrogen and helium
They were massive and seeded heavier elements
Webb sees galaxies from the early universe

questions.prompt: What were the first stars made of?

options.label: The same mix as the Sun today
options.rationale: The Sun contains elements made by earlier stars.

questions.explanation: The first stars formed from the Big Bang’s gas: only hydrogen and helium.

questions.prompt: Why were the first stars important for later planets like Earth?

options.label: They gave off the cosmic microwave background
options.rationale: The CMB was released long before them.

options.label: They became the planets of our solar system
options.rationale: Planets form from gas and dust around stars.

options.label: They made heavier elements and scattered them
They created all the hydrogen in the universe
options.rationale: Hydrogen formed in the Big Bang.

questions.explanation: Rocky planets need heavier elements. The first stars forged some and scattered them into space when they died.

questions.prompt: From Level 36: why do astronomers hunt for the first galaxies in infrared?

options.label: Early galaxies were made of infrared stars
options.rationale: The stars shone normally; their light was stretched later.

options.label: Infrared light travels faster than visible light
options.rationale: All light travels at the same speed.

options.label: Visible light can’t travel that far
options.rationale: Distance alone doesn’t block visible light.

options.label: Their light has been stretched into infrared

questions.explanation: The expanding universe stretched light from early galaxies into infrared wavelengths, so that is where to look.
